extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, students, and anyone studying rhetoric or narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what a 'red herring' is and how it functions as a narrative device and an informal logical fallacy — how to craft plausible-but-irrelevant clues, distinguish the device from related fallacies/devices, and how it is used in fiction, rhetoric, and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — misleads or distracts from relevant question
rubrics_metrics.description: A red herring is something that misleads or distracts from a relevant or important question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a red herring to draw attention away from the central issue; the device can operate in argumentation or narrative. Example phrasing from the page: 'It may be either a logical fallacy or a literary device that leads readers or audiences toward a false conclusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility + irrelevance (what makes it effective)
rubrics_metrics.description: A red herring is a seemingly plausible, though ultimately irrelevant, diversionary tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To work as a red herring, the diversion should feel plausible and connected enough to the main thread that readers/audiences follow it, but in the end it must be irrelevant to the true issue or solution. Example: the word 'Rache' at a crime scene plausibly points to a German motive but is irrelevant to the murderer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional vs unintentional use
rubrics_metrics.description: A red herring may be intentional or unintentional; it is not necessarily a conscious intent to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating work, consider whether the misleading detail was deliberately placed (as a narrative technique or rhetorical tactic) or arose inadvertently (a mistake or irrelevant detail). The Oxford English Dictionary notes both possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from other fallacies/devices (e.g., straw man)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the straw man, which involves a distortion of the other party's position, the red herring is a diversion — a plausible but ultimately irrelevant detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a device, ensure you are deliberately diverting attention (red herring) rather than misrepresenting an opponent's view (straw man). This affects both ethical evaluation (argumentation) and the narrative effect (misdirection vs. distortion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in fiction — false clue to lead readers toward mistaken conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In fiction and non‑fiction, a red herring may be a false clue intended to lead readers or audiences toward a mistaken conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a plot device, place clues that plausibly implicate a character or explanation, then later reveal the truth (e.g., Bishop Aringarosa in The Da Vinci Code; the 'Rache' example in A Study in Scarlet). The device is commonly used in mystery fiction to create suspense and surprise when the diversion is resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical use — red herrings in legal studies/exam problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Red herrings are often used in legal studies and exam problems to mislead and distract students from reaching a correct conclusion about a legal issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting assessment items, add plausible-but-irrelevant facts to test students' ability to identify material facts and apply law rather than be led astray by attractive but irrelevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization as a relevance fallacy (informal fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: As an informal fallacy, the red herring falls into a broad class of relevance fallacies and is mainly used to assert that an argument is not relevant to the issue being discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments, check whether the offered support actually addresses the original issue; if it diverts attention without addressing the point, it functions as a red herring (ignoring the issue qualifies as 'ignoratio elenchi').

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to and distinction from related narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Red herrings are related to other narrative techniques (MacGuffin, Chekhov's gun, foreshadowing, false protagonist, plot twist) but serve a distinct function of intentional misdirection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the device that matches your intended effect: e.g., a MacGuffin motivates action without intrinsic importance, Chekhov's gun promises later payoff, whereas a red herring actively misleads toward a false conclusion. The 'See also' list on the page provides contrastive devices to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/etymological caution — do not assume literal hunting origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The figurative sense was popularized by William Cobbett in 1807, but the literal story of using a smoked herring to distract hounds is likely apocryphal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking origin myths or metaphors for the device, be aware the literal tale is historically contested (e.g., MythBusters tested the hunting idea and found it 'Busted'). This matters when explaining or teaching the device: prefer documented figurative origins over debunked literal anecdotes.
